title: Numbered Art Print: What an Edition of 1/100 Really Means
excerpt: What does "23/100" on an art print actually mean? An honest look at limited editions, value retention, and the psychology behind the number — plus three things you should check before you buy.
content:
You're standing in front of a numbered art print, wondering whether to buy it. In the bottom corner, written in pencil, it says "23/100," with the artist's signature beside it. What does that actually mean? Is the print more valuable because the number is low? Less valuable because 99 other copies exist? The truth is more sober than the art market lets on — and more interesting than Pinterest will tell you.

Here's what a numbered edition really is, what it isn't, and what to look out for before you buy.

What a numbered edition legally is

A limited edition is nothing more than a promise. The artist says: "I'll produce a certain number of copies and then stop." The plate is destroyed, the file deleted, the process shut down.

That promise is contractual and documented through a Certificate of Authenticity — COA for short. If the artist breaks it — secretly reprints, launches a second run, sells digital copies — the work loses its value on the spot. Sometimes the matter ends up in court.

What a numbered edition isn't: a law of nature. The 100 didn't fall from the sky. Someone picked it. The scarcity exists on paper, not in the world.

A quick glossary

  • Edition: The total number of official copies. The "100" in 73/100.
  • AP (Artist's Proof): Extra copies kept for the artist, usually around 10% of the edition. Officially, they don't count as part of the numbered run.
  • HC (Hors Commerce): French for "not for sale." Copies for galleries, archives, or press purposes. They exist, but they aren't for trade.
  • EA (Épreuve d'Artiste): The French version of Artist's Proof. Same idea, different language.
  • Giclée: High-resolution inkjet print on archival paper. The current standard for fine-art prints.
  • Etching: A print pulled from an acid-bitten metal plate. The old method (Rembrandt, Dürer) — rare today, but each impression is more valuable.
  • COA: The Certificate of Authenticity. Lists edition size, number, title, signature, and date.

Why low numbers are often worth more (and why they sometimes aren't)

"1/100 is worth more than 73/100." You'll hear it at fairs, in galleries, on Reddit. Sometimes it's true. Sometimes it isn't. And the reasons are more interesting than the rule itself.

With traditional methods — etching, lithography, screen printing — the plate wears down with every pull. The tenth impression really is sharper than the ninetieth. Here, the number has a tangible, physical basis.

With modern giclée prints, the hundredth impression looks just like the first. Same printer, same file, same paper. The price gap between 1/100 and 73/100 is then pure psychology.

A low number doesn't buy you better print quality. It buys you the feeling of having been there early.

That isn't a bad thing. That feeling is part of what makes art valuable in the first place. You just need to know what you're paying for.

When numbering is marketing — and when it's substance

The number has real meaning when:

  • the edition is genuinely closed and that fact is verifiably documented,
  • the printing process creates physical differences between impressions (etching, lithography),
  • the artist has a name, and an edition of 50 is therefore genuinely scarce and in demand,
  • an independent publisher — a museum, a dedicated edition house — vouches for the process.

The number is pure marketing when:

  • the "limited" edition runs to 5,000 and the artist sells the same motif in ten more sizes,
  • there's no certificate at all — or the certificate comes only from the artist, with no independent verification,
  • the number is handwritten but the print itself was mass-produced industrially,
  • nobody can seriously check whether only 100 copies actually exist.

Three things to check before you buy

1. Is there a complete Certificate of Authenticity?

It should include: title of the work, artist's name, edition size, specific number, printing method, paper quality, date, and signature. Missing half of that? Walk away.

2. Who is the publisher behind it?

A print pulled straight from the artist's studio isn't automatically worse — but it's harder to verify. A publisher or an established gallery has a reputation to lose. Either can be fine. The point is: someone has to stand behind the edition size.

3. What method was used?

Ask directly. Giclée on Hahnemühle 308 gsm? Offset? Lithography? The method tells you more about longevity than any edition number. Pigment ink on archival paper lasts over 100 years. Standard inkjet on photo paper fades in ten.

The special case: very large editions

What happens when the edition isn't 100 copies but 24,236? Does the whole principle collapse?

That was the question that led me to my own project. On i-laugh-you, the edition is precisely one self-portrait — cut into 24,236 numbered fragments. Each fragment shows a different section of the original painting. Each carries a number. Each has its own certificate.

The difference from a classic edition: the fragments aren't identical. Every fragment is a unique piece — it shows a different part of the painting. The number stays, but the logic flips: instead of "1 of 100 identical prints," it's now "one of 24,236 different sections of a single painting."

That's more honest. The scarcity isn't disguised — it's placed in plain sight. A number that high can't pretend to have come about naturally. It's visibly a decision.

What to take away

A numbered art print is worth exactly the sum of three things:

  1. the authenticity is credibly documented,
  2. the print quality holds up over time,
  3. and the artist or publisher has a reputation they'd lose by breaking the rules.

The number in the corner is information, not a guarantee. A 1/500 from a well-known artist on museum paper is usually worth more than a 3/50 from an unknown on standard stock.

Buy the work, not the number. The number only proves that somebody bothered to count.

And if you want to see what an edition looks like when it owns up to its own artificiality: click your way through the canvas of i-laugh-you. There, the number 24,236 isn't hidden — it's the whole subject.
